title: Fed's Warsh says AI path will be 'very bumpy' but ultimately 'very good' for wealth
titleJa: Fed's Warsh says AI path will be 'very bumpy' but ultimately 'very good' for wealth
summaryJa: Warsh said he's optimistic that AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, warning the road there will be "very bumpy."
bodyOriginal:
BANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said he's optimistic that artificial intelligence will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, though he warned the road there will be "very bumpy" and its near-term effect on jobs is unknown.
Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
"I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said. A decade from now, he said, people will look back "and say this was hugely consequential."
The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023. A communication blackout period starts later Friday, ahead of its Oct. 27-28 meeting.
Warsh also said the global economy has "broadly conformed" to the central bank's expectations since its September rate increase, but he declined to say what he will do at the coming meeting. "I don't prejudge meetings," he said.
Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged, according to CME Fed Watch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

title: Hybe shares jump 10% as K-pop sensation BTS' tour lifts earnings hopes
titleJa: Hybe shares jump 10% as K-pop sensation BTS' tour lifts earnings hopes
summaryJa: BTS' world tour and rising global demand for newer K-pop acts are fueling earnings expectations, sending Hybe shares soaring.
bodyOriginal:
Shares of Hybe, the company behind K-pop supergroup BTS, surged 10% on Friday as investors weighed an upbeat third-quarter earnings outlook fueled by its artistes' global concerts.
Hybe's third-quarter revenue is expected to reach 1.5 trillion won ($1.11 billion), up 106% from a year earlier, while operating profit is projected at 172.2 billion won, according to local brokerage firm iM Securities. Concert revenue is expected to come in at 717 billion won, nearly tripling from a year earlier.
The share price gain on Friday outperformed the broader Kospi, which rose 2.9%.
BTS' ongoing world tour featured 16 stadium shows in North America and eight in Europe during the third quarter.
Thiat, alongside expanding tours by newer acts including Enhypen, Katseye and Cortis, helped drive concert attendance to nearly 3 million during the quarter, potentially marking a quarterly record for the company, the report said.
Western markets accounted for more than 70% of total concert attendance for the first time, reflecting Hybe's growing international reach as its newer artistes expand their presence in North America and Europe, according to the report. Despite currency headwinds, concert, merchandise and licensing revenues are expected to reach record levels.
Concert margin outlook
While higher royalty payments to established artistes and initial touring costs for newer groups are expected to weigh on margins, the brokerage forecasts Hybe to maintain a double-digit operating margin, supported by the scale of BTS' world tour.
CGS Securities analyst Jiwoo Oh told CNBC after Hybe's second-quarter earnings that while concerts and appearances carry steeper costs for the company due to higher revenue sharing with artistes, merchandise, content and fan club businesses help boost the companies bottom line significantly.
She also pointed out that in its second quarter, Hybe delivered an 11.8% operating margin in the second quarter of 2026, with artist-direct revenue accounting for 72% of total sales and concerts alone accounting for 45% of total sales.
"We believe this demonstrates that stadium-scale operating leverage can more than offset the higher cost base associated with concerts," she added.
After Hybe reported second-quarter results on July 28, the company's shares crashed, wiping out as much as $1.96 billion in market cap in less than 24 hours.
Analysts said then that the sell-off was caused as profit margins missed expectations, despite revenue and operating profit reaching record highs, according to analysts.
Rookies step up
The iM Securities report said that the profitability of newer bands such as Katseye and Cortis in Western markets will be likely key to reducing the company's reliance on BTS, the report showed.
Still, stronger-than-expected demand for additional BTS concerts in Japan and the Middle East, as well as encore performances, could also lead to upward revisions to the company's 2027 earnings forecasts, iM Securities added.
Kyobo Securities, which expects third-quarter concert revenue to reach 724.4 billion won, expressed optimism around Hybe's newer acts, stating "growth among younger artists is becoming more visible alongside BTS' tour."
Cortis is selling around 600,000 albums per month on average, demonstrating strong fandom demand, the brokerage said, while Katseye is expanding its overseas presence on the back of global streaming and album performance.

title: Russia returns to G20 table in Bangkok on U.S. invitation that angers Europe
titleJa: Russia returns to G20 table in Bangkok on U.S. invitation that angers Europe
summaryJa: Russia’s return to the G20 table has tested how far Washington’s outreach to Moscow will strain ties with European allies.
bodyOriginal:
Russia's finance minister attended a Group of 20 meeting in Bangkok on Thursday, his second in-person appearance at the event since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, testing how far Washington's rapprochement with Moscow will strain ties with Europe.
Anton Siluanov and Bank of Russia Deputy Governor Elizaveta Danilova were listed as Russia's delegates at the finance ministers and central bank governors' meetings on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, according to a seating plan seen by CNBC. Siluanov was in the meeting, according to a person familiar with the matter.
According to the layout document, Russian delegates were seated between attendees from South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil was also listed as an attendee. At the August G20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, he told Siluanov that Moscow must end the war and declined to pose in a group photo with him. The traditional group photo was ultimately taken without the Russian delegation after European officials protested.
Klingbeil has pushed back on the U.S. efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage, reportedly saying after the Thursday meeting that "there will be no pretending that Russia is now returning as a normal member of the G20 and simply taking its seat at the table again — not with me, and not with the other Europeans."
Russia's seat at the table tests how far Washington can ease pressure on Moscow without breaking with its European allies. The U.S., which took over the G20 presidency this year, welcomed Russia's finance minister back to the finance talks after years of isolation over the invasion of Ukraine.
The Trump administration also introduced a deal to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel imports until April, drawing criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies. Dombrovskis told CNBC on Wednesday that "now it's not a time to ease sanctions on Russia."
In a statement issued after the Thursday meetings, Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers said Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on commercial vessels "must end." Those impacts "are exacerbated by Russia's unprovoked and unjustifiable war in Ukraine," he said, adding that Australia calls for Russia to end the war and respect Ukraine's sovereignty.
The finance chiefs ended the meeting without a joint communique, underscoring persistent divisions among members over the Middle East conflict, trade imbalances, and Russia's war with Ukraine. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who would normally chair the talks, skipped the meetings to stay in Washington.
The Asheville meeting also ended without a communique, after China objected to language on several issues, including efforts to rectify excessive global trade surpluses. The U.S. instead issued a chair's statement backed by every member present except China, with Bessent calling China "the dissenter."
Delegates started the day with a plated breakfast of baked goat cheese, spinach and egg soufflé with chutney made from locally grown Bijin tomatoes, according to a menu card at the venue. The bread basket came with "Nam Dok Mai" mango jam. Every card carried the U.S. presidency's stars-and-stripes G20 logo and its "Freedom 250" tagline, marking America's 250th anniversary.
The finance ministers' meeting Thursday could have helped lay the groundwork for improved coordination on a raft of global challenges, including energy problems stemming from the Middle East conflict and concerns about record public debt in advanced economies. Leaders are expected to convene at the next G20 summit in Miami in December.

title: Living with a stink? Technology might help
titleJa: Living with a stink? Technology might help
summaryJa: Smells from rubbish dumps and industrial facilities are being more carefully monitored.
bodyOriginal:
Living with a stink? Technology might help
- Published
Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem.
For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill.
"When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump.
While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day".
Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology.
The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells.
Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts."
The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality.
Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory.
When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells.
In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue.
Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance.
This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks.
"You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world.
The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away.
Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells.
But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.
Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner.
Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says.
In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city.
A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits.
"Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume."
The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus.
The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns.
This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?"
Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems.
Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints.
Before installing the monitors – which some local companies help pay for – officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air.
Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios Obregón from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic."
The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it easier to detect smells.
Whatever technology is used, it can be hard to keep everyone happy, as smells are so subjective. "Unfortunately, the general rule is that the nastier we perceive the odour to be, the more sensitive towards it we are," says Johan Lundström, a professor in the science of smell at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.

title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
titleJa: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
summaryJa: After Primark announced plans for home delivery, we hear from women who never go into clothes stores.
bodyOriginal:
I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
- Published
Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online.
As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says.
"The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough.
Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on".
And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection".
Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22.
But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain.
Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases.
The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.
Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.
Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic.
Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019.
Internet shopping has also been boosted by the decline of the High Street in many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town."
'I basically never go into clothes shops'
Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online.
"I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says.
"I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important."
Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted.
The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces."
Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically.
"I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed."
The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule.
Returns policy can 'make or break'
Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale".
However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete.
"Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks.
"When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time."
But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns.
This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor".
"Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again."

But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain.
Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases.
The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.
Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.
Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic.
Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019.
Internet shopping has also been boosted by the decline of the High Street in many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town."
'I basically never go into clothes shops'
Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online.
"I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says.
"I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important."
Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted.
The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces."
Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically.
"I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed."
The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule.
Returns policy can 'make or break'
Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale".
However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete.
"Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks.
"When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time."
But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns.
This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor".
"Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again."

title: Netflix Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria is leaving, will be replaced by Peter Rice
titleJa: Netflix Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria is leaving, will be replaced by Peter Rice
summaryJa: Netflix announced Bela Bajaria will be replaced by former Disney exec Peter Rice as the company's chief content officer.
bodyOriginal:
Netflix on Thursday announced Bela Bajaria will be replaced as the company's chief content officer by former Disney exec Peter Rice, effective Oct. 26.
Rice most recently oversaw Disney's cable channels, news programming and coverage of major sporting events.
"Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry," co-CEO Ted Sarandos said in a statement. "I'm excited to welcome him to Netflix as Chief Content Officer as we continue to scale and deliver members more of the stories they love."
Before Rice was at Disney, he held roles at 21st Century Fox and Fox Searchlight Pictures. Netflix in its announcement called him "one of the entertainment industry's most respected creative executives." In his new role, Rice will oversee the company's global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events.
"[Netflix has] shown again and again that they're willing to take chances on distinctive voices and fresh ideas, and I'm excited to work with the team to help bring even more great stories to members everywhere," he said in a statement.
Bajaria, who is leaving Netflix after nearly 10 years, most recently led the company's global content team. She had been focused on the company's live sports strategy, looking to create events out of buzzy games and tournaments.
"I'm incredibly grateful for everything she's done to help Netflix entertain the world," Sarandos said in a statement.

The media company will report its next quarterly earnings on Tuesday.

title: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
titleJa: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
summaryJa: KFC is switching from PepsiCo to Coca-Cola as its beverage supplier for U.S. restaurants.
bodyOriginal:
KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.
Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.
The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes.
"This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."
For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House, its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas.
Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.
KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.
Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.
For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands.
It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

title: Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity
titleJa: Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity
summaryJa: Porsche revealed a concept car called Mission S as part of a turnaround plan that includes efforts to boost profits through higher-end products and lower sales.
bodyOriginal:
Porsche on Thursday revealed a concept car called Mission S that signals a new design direction and flagship model for the famed German sports carmaker.
The debut of the sleek midengine vehicle is part of a turnaround plan revealed last week by the Volkswagen-controlled brand that includes efforts to boost profits through higher-end products and lower vehicle sales.
Porsche described Mission S as "a first glimpse of the brand's evolved design identity" that also represents a "super sports car platform" that will be positioned above its iconic 911 sports car.
The vehicle's design is recognizably Porsche but with more aggressive styling compared with its current models, including new hood vents and a roof scoop. Its rear features more differentiated flair in which the vehicle's spoiler flows into its rear panels.
"A Porsche must be recognisable as a Porsche at first glance," Porsche Chairman Michael Leiters said in a release. "The Mission S provides a glimpse of the ideas and design features that will shape Porsche in the coming years."
Automakers routinely use concept vehicles to gauge customer interest, showcase future technologies and signal the direction of a vehicle or brand.
The company did not release expected pricing or performance specifications for such future models. Starting prices for its current 911 models range from roughly $135,500 for an entry-level Carrera to more than $203,000 for a Carrera 4 GTS convertible.
During Porsche's capital markets day on Oct. 7, the company outlined its "Sportwagenschmiede '35" turnaround plan, which focuses on emphasizing high-end sports cars and luxury SUVs to get the carmaker back on track.
Porsche's operating margin last year was only 1.1%, compared with 14.1% in 2024, as the company deals with increased costs, U.S. tariffs and declining sales in China.
The turnaround plan includes a long-term target for a group operating margin of 15% and a midterm breakeven point of 200,000 units or below annually. That compares with sales of 279,449 in 2025.

title: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
titleJa: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
summaryJa: CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure buildout. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.
bodyOriginal:
CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.
CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure buildout. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.
Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.
Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.
Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.
Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.
While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.
Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.
Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.
The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.
A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.
"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.
'Self-fulfilling prophecy'
CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.
"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."
The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.
"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.
Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.
"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

title: Tesla plans next-generation Roadster reveal after almost a decade of delays
titleJa: Tesla plans next-generation Roadster reveal after almost a decade of delays
summaryJa: Elon Musk first debuted the Roadster refresh concept in 2017 but Tesla has since missed every targeted delivery date.
bodyOriginal:
Tesla is planning to show off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car.
The event will be livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco. It's expected to begin at 7:55 local time (8:55 ET).
Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, used a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012.
The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology, such as cold gas thrusters, to enable it to hover. Musk fanatics have been gearing up for the demonstration, expressing their excitement on social media, but the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company.
Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Executives are expected to disclose specific pricing, details and production targets.
Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017, and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly."
Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either.
Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his own reservation and refund requests.
"I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait."
Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court over a separate matter earlier this year related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure.
Others have kept their reservations.
Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000.
O'Connor wrote in a message that he plans to attend Thursday's event and is "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making."
According to filings with the Federal Aviation Administration, Tesla established a no-fly zone around the SpaceX facility where it plans to show off the vehicle. The company had to scrap a demo on Oct. 1 due to weather issues.
Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.

title: U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters
titleJa: U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters
summaryJa: The lawsuit by the Trump administration comes less than a month before the midterm election that will determine which party controls both chambers of Congress.
bodyOriginal:
The federal government sued the state of California on Thursday in an escalating battle over how to prevent non-U.S. citizens from voting by mail in federal elections.

title: The problem with 'good debt': Why borrowers should think twice about the label
titleJa: The problem with 'good debt': Why borrowers should think twice about the label
summaryJa: Mortgages and student loans are often called "good debt." Experts say that label can hide the real question: Can you actually afford the risk?
bodyOriginal:
When Bryanna Hambrick bought a three-bedroom, two-bathroom single-family home in Columbus, Ohio, in 2022, she hoped that life milestone would help her save money on rent and build wealth.
"Society puts a lot of pressure on you to have property, get married, have kids," said the 35-year-old. "Life wasn't giving me those other things, so I was like, well, I can buy a home. I can control that."
But her purchase came with a monthly payment of nearly $1,200, about $200 more than expected, after a property tax reassessment and a higher-than-anticipated interest rate on her mortgage. Much of her savings went toward closing costs, Hambrick said, while expensive and unexpected home repairs have kept her living paycheck to paycheck in the years since.
"Anytime I've gotten a certain dollar amount in my savings that makes me feel a little bit more comfortable, something happens," Hambrick said.
Hambrick's experience highlights what experts say is a broader problem: Even debt that seems like a sound investment can become a financial burden.
Mortgages and student loans are often called "good debt" because they may help borrowers build wealth or increase their earning power. "Bad debt," by contrast, often includes credit card balances as well as auto and personal loans, because they often finance consumption or assets that can lose value.
But financial experts say the "good debt" label can downplay the risk for borrowers and lead them to overextend themselves, making repayment challenging.
"I try to avoid talking about 'good debt' now," said Sheila Bair, an author and advisor who chaired the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation from 2006 to 2011. "I think your presumption should always be against debt ... it's a burden on your financial future, and there are a lot of ways it's marketed that make it look like it's not."
Look beyond the 'good debt' label
Even if a purchase seems to check all the boxes, you need to consider the long term. "Young people shouldn't feel pressured to buy a home or borrow to go to college," said Bair, a member of the CNBC Global Financial Wellness Advisory Board and former president of Washington College. "It's a decision that needs to make sense for you financially, and for some people, it won't."
She recommends asking yourself whether taking on debt will improve your financial well-being. Then dig into the details.
For example, whether a mortgage is financially sound depends on factors including the home price, loan terms, and the borrower's income stability and financial reserves.
Experts say you should do your own calculations to figure out how much mortgage payment you feel comfortable with. Don't expect lenders to tell you how much house you can afford; mortgage companies consider what you can repay, not what's in your budget.
"Make sure your mortgage is affordable before you do anything else, and make sure you're going to be there for many years, because home prices over time will appreciate in value, but they go up and down," said Bair. She recommends planning to live in the home for at least five years to account for transaction costs and the possibility of short-term price declines.
The housing crash that precipitated the 2008 financial crisis shows how debt commonly viewed as "good" can go bad. Average U.S. home prices rose sharply between 1998 and 2006 as mortgage lending expanded, including to borrowers with weaker credit. Some borrowers took on large mortgages, betting that home values would keep rising.
"A lot of the folks that had those subprime mortgages didn't understand what they were getting," said Bair.
When home prices fell and payments rose on some adjustable-rate mortgages, foreclosures surged. There were about 3.8 million foreclosures between 2007 and 2010, according to an analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.
Why even 'good' debt can become a mistake
Beyond the fundamentals such as interest rates and repayment terms, borrowers should examine their motivations and expectations before taking on debt, said Brad Klontz, a financial psychologist and certified financial planner.
Many people get tripped up by impulse borrowing, tying self-worth to big purchases, and too-rosy expectations about future earnings, he said.
"We have some chronic debt mistakes that we're all vulnerable to," said Klontz, who is a member of the CNBC Financial Advisor Council and the CNBC Global Financial Wellness Advisory Board.
He recommends people approach debt as a business decision — and temper their expectations. If, say, buying a home or getting a master's degree has the potential to generate wealth, don't automatically assume it will; consider the risk and return on that investment, he said.
Make sure your assumptions aren't overly optimistic. For example, when considering education spending, research potential careers and salaries in the government's Occupational Outlook Handbook. Then work backward and ask: "Does it make sense for me to take on student loan debt to get a degree? Do you even need a degree?" Klontz said.
Avoid emotional borrowing to fund a lifestyle, impress others, or pay for short-term experiences, said Klontz.
"If you're taking on debt to travel, that is a financial mistake," Klontz said. Instead, he suggests planning and saving for travel experiences. "A lot of times, when people are overspending or taking on debt for a vacation, it's somewhat of an impulse purchase." That can lead to long-term regret, he said, "because you're having that emotional experience, and then you come back home to reality, and now you're stuck with the chronic stress of trying to pay that off."
Klontz said one of the biggest mistakes he sees people make is buying the "absolute biggest, best house [they] can possibly afford."
"Even people who are really wise with money fall into that mistake," Klontz said. They may overestimate their ability to make more money in the future and underestimate how much they will spend on repairs and maintenance, he said.
Hambrick said she wishes she had focused more on the cost of the home than the hardwood floors and granite countertops. "Your first house doesn't have to be your forever home," she said.
Hambrick's home value has appreciated, but not as much as she expected. "It feels like bad debt, bad decision overall," she said.
— CNBC's Nathaniel Lee contributed reporting.

title: Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits
titleJa: Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits
summaryJa: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect to be "on the menu" in the chancellor's Budget tax later this month.
bodyOriginal:
Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits
- Published
Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect the sector to be "on the menu" when the chancellor announces his Budget in two weeks' time.
John Healey has described the banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, yet has refused to rule out a raid on the sector.
The biggest four banks collectively made around £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, leading to calls from trade unions and others for additional taxes.
However, the banking sector trade body, UK Finance, warned that "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".
The UK's biggest banks and building societies currently pay a surcharge of 3% on top of the baseline 25% rate of corporation tax, plus a levy on the assets held on their balance sheets.
The sector contributed nearly £40bn to the Treasury last year, if income tax on employees is factored in.
The bank levy generated £1.4bn last year and the surcharge a further £1.2bn.
There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.
The 3% surcharge was reduced from 8% under Rishi Sunak, at the same time as he raised corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Returning the surcharge to its previous level could raise around £2bn a year.
The bank levy currently charges 0.1% on outstanding short-term loans and 0.05% on longer-dated loans, although mortgages are excluded from the calculation.
In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.
In truth, banks were pleasantly surprised they were not hit at the last Budget, given the large profits they have been making in recent years. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which they lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.
There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.
Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.
It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.
However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.
Whatever form it takes, banks believe the chancellor now has much more of an appetite to take a larger slice of their pie.

title: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
titleJa: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
summaryJa: Ukraine's president says a pause on striking energy sites is over following fresh Russian attacks.
bodyOriginal:
Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
- Published
Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery after Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume.
Ukraine's president said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia had continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external.
Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing on Russian strikes to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks altogether after it struck a deal to import Russian diesel, and he said curbs on Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine's military were deliberate.
Ukrainian defence sources told the BBC some Starlink functionality had resumed as of Thursday morning.
They said its military service Starshield's "operation while on the move" had been restored, although it remains unclear whether the restrictions to the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection have been fully lifted.
Officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances" behind the move, the sources added.
In a separate development, seven people are missing after a drone attack set a chemical tanker on fire off Romania, according to naval officials. Moscow said it had hit two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port, without naming them.
Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
- Published5 hours ago
Eight crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
- Published2 hours ago
The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.
According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.
President Vladimir Putin said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine has denied - and had not caused "significant damage" so far.
Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.
He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.
But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal.
Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.
European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake".
"Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself."
He added: "Peace will be achieved when Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war."
Zelensky met Nato chief Mark Rutte as a two-day summit of European leaders began in Brussels on Thursday. The head of the military alliance said they had discussed "the importance of implementing an energy ceasefire as well as Nato allies' continuous support for Ukraine".
Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".
Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.
There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggested it was the Trump administration's doing.
"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.
Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment.
Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv.
The Ukrainian president told the newspaper he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles.
Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles.
Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Putin.
He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week: "We didn't destroy any relationship."
Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.
Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.
But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.
That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.
Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."
With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.
Local officials report at least 13 people were killed across Ukraine on Wednesday in what Zelensky called a "constant", large-scale Russian attack. He said more than 850 drones had been launched at dozens of cities and communities.
At least three people were killed in the central region of Kirovohrad as it suffered its largest attack since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, officials there said, with nearly 360 drones launched during a 10-hour barrage. Deaths were also reported in Donetsk, Kherson and Volyn.
"It is clear that Russia deliberately escalated these attacks, taking advantage of the easing of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelensky wrote on social media.

title: International Energy Agency to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible
titleJa: International Energy Agency to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible
summaryJa: The Trump administration pushed Europe to release diesel stocks as prices in the U.S. surged to record highs in September.
bodyOriginal:
International Energy Agency members have agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel "as soon as possible" as fuel prices surge globally, the group said in a statement Thursday.
President Donald Trump said earlier this month that Europe had agreed to deploy a "massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil." The release detailed by the IEA on Thursday is equivalent to less than one day of global diesel demand or slightly more than five days of U.S. consumption.
The IEA did not specify a timeline for the release in its Thursday statement. The Group of Seven nations led by France said on Oct. 2 that they would deploy substantial diesel stocks over 20 days. If that is the IEA's timeline, its members would supply about 1 million barrels each day for almost three weeks.
Diesel futures are trading more than 1% lower Thursday at $4.86.
The IEA, headquartered in Paris, has more than 30 member states, including the U.S. and key European and Asian allies. The agency, created in 1974 in the wake of the Arab oil embargo, is tasked with maintaining energy security by deploying oil stockpiles in response to crises like the wars in the Middle East and Eastern Europe.
The Trump administration has pushed Europe to release diesel inventories as prices in the U.S. surged to record highs in September. The retail price of diesel stood at an average $6.32 per gallon Thursday, more than 70% above the same period last year, according to AAA.
Trump is facing political pressure to address fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. The president struck a diesel deal with Russia last week that analysts have said will do little to reduce prices.
The G7 nations, led by France, announced earlier this month that they would deploy stocks through the IEA in response to the diesel crisis but did not give specific quantities.
The IEA release does "not solve the basic problem which is how to increase production at refineries which are damaged in the Middle East or Russia, and operating at capacity in the USA," said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.
Prices have surged as Ukraine has pounded Russian refineries and Iran and its Houthi allies have attacked energy facilities around the Persian Gulf.
IEA members agreed in March to deploy 400 million barrels of oil in response to the global supply disruption triggered by the Iran war. They have since agreed to release the remaining 100 million barrels pledged in March "in a timely manner consistent with national circumstances," the group said Thursday.
IEA's governing board said 330 million barrels have been released so far. Some members have deployed more than they originally pledged so the total release will exceed the 400 million barrels agreed in March.

title: Banks with Jeffrey Epstein ties eyed by Democrats Warren and Garcia
titleJa: Banks with Jeffrey Epstein ties eyed by Democrats Warren and Garcia
summaryJa: Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Robert Garcia are leading new legislation to force banks and some executives to release records related to Jeffrey Epstein.
bodyOriginal:
Financial institutions and bank executives that may have aided the late financier Jeffrey Epstein's sex trafficking operation are in the sights of a bipartisan group of lawmakers.
Legislation introduced Thursday — and led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif. — would require financial regulators to produce records related to Epstein, compel those regulators to investigate banks and executives with ties to the deceased convicted sex offender, and require industry bans and civil penalties for those found to have aided him.
"I have spent the last year calling on Donald Trump's financial regulators to launch investigations into the big banks and executives who may have enabled Jeffrey Epstein's horrific crimes," Warren, who leads the Senate banking committee's Democrats, said in a statement. "Since they have failed to act, Congress must. The bipartisan Epstein Wall Street Records Act will ensure overdue accountability for the wealthy and well-connected on Wall Street who put profits over people."
The legislation is co-led in the House by Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill. Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., signed on to the Senate version. The House version has 17 Democratic co-sponsors.
The proposal would apply to the Federal Reserve, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, Treasury's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Securities and Exchange Commission. A spokesperson for the Federal Reserve declined to comment. Spokespeople for the other regulators did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Since the start of Trump's second term, Democrats and a small group of Republicans have pressed the president to release records related to Epstein and to investigate the individuals and businesses associated with him.
Warren has sought answers from Barclays, Goldman Sachs, and JP Morgan Chase on their connections to Epstein. And Wyden, in his capacity as the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, released an investigation in August that found "significant evidence that JPMorgan, Deutsche Bank, and Bank of America violated federal anti-money laundering laws by failing to screen and report Epstein's suspicious financial transactions in a timely manner."
Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan Chase both declined to comment on Thursday. Barclays did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The fallout from the Epstein files has been politically perilous for Republicans, who largely opposed an effort, led by Massie and Khanna, to force a vote to release the documents. After Trump belatedly signaled his support for the legislation, the Epstein Files Transparency Act passed both chambers of Congress with near unanimity and was signed into law in November 2025. The legislation was meant to force the Department of Justice to release its records related to Epstein.
But ahead of November's midterm election, Democrats in recent weeks have ramped up campaign ads hitting their GOP opponents for past opposition to releasing the Epstein files. And those who advocated for public disclosure of the files have continued to push for accountability in Washington and on Wall Street.
"The Epstein Files Transparency Act forced the Attorney General to release DOJ, FBI, and U.S. Attorney's Offices' files. This bill does the same for bank regulators. Justice for the survivors means following the money," Massie, who had a falling out with Trump over his effort to release the Epstein files, said in a statement.

title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
titleJa: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
summaryJa: Trump said some would "rather not watch" the killing of Nidal Hasan, the first military execution in over 60 years.
bodyOriginal:
Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
- Published
US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.
Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.
Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".
"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added.
Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at a military base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish.
"They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said.
After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others. The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent".
While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. According to Amnesty International, 11 public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".
But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.
The president also called Hasan "totally nuts".
"I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him," he said.
John Galligan, a lawyer for Hasan working primarily on civil issues, told the BBC that Trump's decision to cancel the livestream of his execution "comes as no surprise".
"It was initially a dumb decision and statement by Hegseth to livestream any execution - and it violated the Army's own regulation," Galligan said.
He said Hasan is paralysed from the chest down, something that Trump "allegedly didn't even know" when he approved the livestream plan.
"The damage has already been done - the Army is now just trying to clean up the mess," Galligan said. "It will permanently remain a stain on our military justice system."
He added that it was not clear if Hasan was aware yet of Trump's "reversal" of the livestream decision.
Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
US military law requires that a military execution be approved by the US president. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward.

title: Wholesale prices jumped 6.3% annually in September, biggest gain since 2022
titleJa: Wholesale prices jumped 6.3% annually in September, biggest gain since 2022
summaryJa: September producer prices were expected to increase 0.6% month over month and 5.5% annually, according to the consensus estimate by Dow Jones.
bodyOriginal:
September's producer price index came in much hotter than economists forecast on Thursday, underscoring the continued inflationary pressure from energy amid the U.S. war with Iran.
The measure of underlying inflation pressures climbed 1.3% in September and 6.3% on an annual basis, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That marked the largest monthly and annual gains since March 2022 and December 2022, respectively.
Both readings topped expectations of economists polled by Dow Jones, who forecast an advance of 0.6% on the month and 5.5% annually.
Energy drove a sizable chunk of those increases as the Middle East conflict curtailed oil supply and sent prices surging. The so-called core PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices from the wholesaler inflation index, added 0.7% on the month and 5% over the 12-month period.
But there are signs that soaring energy prices are having downstream effects on other categories. The BLS said in Thursday's release that almost half of September's increase in processed goods for immediate demand was connected to the rise in diesel fuel prices.
It's the latest report in recent days showing that inflation continues to hit consumers and companies.
Wednesday's consumer price index release showed a rise of 0.6% from August to September and 3.7% on a 12-month basis. Economists polled by Dow Jones had forecast growth of 0.6% and 3.6%, respectively.
Excluding food and energy, the core CPI added 0.3% on the month and 2.6% compared with a year ago. Economists anticipated increases of 0.2% and 2.5%, respectively.
Wednesday's Beige Book, a chronicle of economic activity published by the Federal Reserve, had the highest number of mentions of terms related to inflation on record, according to an analysis from Bespoke Investment Group.
Retail sales grew 0.8% in September, surpassing the rate of 0.4% anticipated by economists, according to government data released in a separate report Thursday. That marked a slowdown from a month prior, when retail sales rose by more than 1%.
Excluding spending on autos and gas stations, retail sales increased 0.25% from August to September, a drop from around 1.1% in the prior period. This slowdown offers a sign that high prices related to fuel are causing consumers to tighten the belt elsewhere.
This week's data has left a growing minority of fed funds futures traders expecting the central bank to raise rates at its meeting later this month. Traders are now pricing in a nearly 34% likelihood that the Fed hikes borrowing costs on Oct. 28, up from under 18% a week prior, according to CME's FedWatch tool. About 90% expect at least one hike by the end of the year.
"With a second day in a row of higher-than-expected inflation numbers, it seems the Fed will have no choice but to raise rates again this year," said Chris Zaccarelli, investing chief at Northlight Asset Management.
These reports offer some of the final insights into the pace of inflation in the U.S. ahead of the midterm election, which could impact how much power each political party has in Washington.

title: TSMC chip capacity is ‘fierce’ battleground for AI customers, amid record quarter
titleJa: TSMC chip capacity is ‘fierce’ battleground for AI customers, amid record quarter
summaryJa: TSMC had a record quarter, but it can't make chips for everyone as Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom and AMD fight for capacity.
bodyOriginal:
As Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.'s record quarter makes clear, demand from chipmakers shows no sign of slowing down. In fact, TSMC can't manufacture quickly enough.
The artificial intelligence boom has created unending need for space on factory lines at the world's leading chip manufacturer, and it could put a chokehold on the entire industry's ability to scale. Last year, TSMC said it had the capacity to make more than 17 million 12-inch equivalent wafers. But customers want more.
"The competition is extremely fierce," said Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities. "It's a game of who can get the most leverage and supply."
TSMC makes the vast majority of the world's most advanced semiconductors, the graphics processors and central processors from Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom that are necessary for running AI workloads. Now a growing number of tech firms – Apple, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and OpenAI – also rely on TSMC to make custom in-house AI accelerators.
TSMC North American CEO Sajiv Dalal told CNBC he gets at least 10 calls a day about wafer capacity. TSMC posted record profit for a sixth straight quarter on Thursday and expects fourth-quarter revenue to be 58% higher than a year earlier, driven by strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies.
If compute demand continues to grow at the current rate over the next 12 to 18 months, Klein said capacity constraints at TSMC could threaten some of the industry's massive infrastructure investments and the "aggressive revenue growth targets" from the AI companies. U.S. hyperscalers are projecting well over $700 billion in capital expenditures this year, and analysts expect that figure to jump in 2027.
AI ambitions are also threatened by a global shortage of memory chips. The logic chips that TSMC manufactures are more complex and expensive to produce. That means GPU and CPU leaders like Nvidia and AMD work out lengthy contracts and bespoke deals with TSMC behind closed doors years in advance. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su have both visited Taiwan multiple times this year.
Sid Sheth, CEO of AI chip startup D-Matrix, has fostered a relationship with TSMC for more than 20 years, and his company relies on TSMC to manufacture its processors. Sheth said that for TSMC customers, many roads lead to Kevin Zhang, a senior vice president of the Taiwanese company and a central figure in determining which chipmakers get access to its coveted factory lines.
He's "currently probably the most popular person on the planet," Sheth said in an interview. Sheth said that Jerry Qubain, D-Matrix's vice president of manufacturing, has been visiting TSMC since 1992 and goes to Taiwan three to four times a year.
"This was even before Nvidia was founded," Sheth said. "That's a good example of a person we brought on board because of the relationships he has at TSMC." Qubain joined D-Matrix in 2024. TSMC declined to participate in this story.
Betting on startups
TSMC had 534 customers in 2025. While it doesn't name or rank them, its top 10 customers accounted for 78% of net revenue, with its top two bringing in 19% and 17%, respectively.
That leaves startups competing for capacity against customers with far bigger orders. Sheth said TSMC is "selective," but has an incentive to back promising newcomers.
"They were very supportive of Nvidia and Broadcom when they were very young companies, and now these are their biggest customers today," Sheth said. "They want to see a repeat of that."
TSMC is hustling to bring much more capacity online, with new fabs in Taiwan, Japan and Arizona — it's making advanced chips in the U.S. for the first time. In July, TSMC announced it was adding $100 billion and "several more" fabs to the six planned in Arizona, bringing its total commitment to $265 billion. TSMC is also reportedly considering an entirely new fab location in Texas.

title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
titleJa: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
summaryJa: The culture secretary says the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.
bodyOriginal:
Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
- Published
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.
Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.
Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal.
"We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.
ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries".
The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.
The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.
It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix.
What Sky buying ITV could mean for your favourite shows
- Published6 July
But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up.
In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including:
The need for free expression of opinion in news media
The need for a range of views in news media across the UK
The need for a range of people controlling the media across the UK
The need for a wide range of programmes to be offered across the UK
The letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV.
Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added.
But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV.
The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued.
This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added.
Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns.
A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."
An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process.
"This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries."
Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration.
This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes.
She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."
